A discounted rights issue still needs cash: reconcile entitlement value and subscription funding

Four charts explain a theoretical ex-rights price, the value attached to an existing holding, funded exercise versus sale or lapse, and the cash required for a proportional subscription.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 5 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Separate theoretical rights value from the cash required to subscribe

Interactive planning lab

Cash required to subscribe to the full entitlement$150
Theoretical value of the holding’s rights$80
Additional outside cash required before subscribing$0

An independently authored, fully subscribed, pro-rata rights-issue benchmark; no company, security quote or actual offer is evaluated. The offer grants one new share per selected number of old shares. Subscription price is the entered old quote less its selected percentage discount. Existing business value is assumed unchanged; new subscription cash adds value dollar for dollar and all company new shares are ultimately taken up, regardless of this holder’s choice. The theoretical ex-rights price is (ratio × old quote + subscription price) / (ratio + 1), not a forecast of trading price. The eligible holding’s entitlement is calculated proportionally, including mathematical fractional new shares with no rounding or dealing restriction. Rights are assumed transferable and sold at the calculated theoretical value without fees in the sale scenario. Lapse receives no compensation. Neither term applies universally to actual offers. No issue fee, tax, spread, price movement, deadline date, receipt delay, interest, corporate-value change or tax cost basis is calculated. The outside cash is the only funding available to exercise; no asset sale or borrowing is invented. The entered cash covers the modeled full subscription. Resource totals include the same opening shares and outside cash in every displayed alternative. They are static theoretical comparisons, not guaranteed executable transactions, income or a judgment about whether participation is suitable.

The central idea

A right can have value without being cash available to subscribe. Reconcile the old holding, the entitlement and new capital separately before interpreting a discounted subscription as an extra return.

01

Separate the invitation to subscribe from the money needed to do it

A rights issue can allow existing shareholders to buy additional shares in proportion to their holdings. The entitlement and the subscription cash are different resources: having the right does not mean the holder already has the money required to exercise it.

FINRA's corporate-action explanation describes that general structure. ASX's glossary distinguishes rights that may be traded from non-renounceable rights that cannot be traded. Those sources supply terminology rather than terms for an actual offer here.

The default illustration assumes an eligible holding of one hundred shares quoted at CAD 10 before the rights detach. The offer allows one new share for every four old shares, with a subscription price 40% below the entered old quote.

The example assumes the company ultimately issues all of the new shares and receives all subscription cash, regardless of this holder's choice. Existing business value does not change, and cash raised adds value dollar for dollar. These are deliberately restrictive valuation assumptions, not a prediction about a company raising capital.

02

Calculate the enlarged-share benchmark before reading the discount as a return

The subscription price is CAD 6 per new share. Consider a normalized group of four old shares worth CAD 40 before the issue. Adding one new share and CAD 6 of subscription capital creates five shares backed by CAD 46 in this benchmark.

The theoretical ex-rights price is therefore (4 × CAD 10 + CAD 6) ÷ 5 = CAD 9.20. It is a weighted capital calculation, not an observed market quote or a price at which a trade is guaranteed.

The holder's full entitlement is twenty-five new shares and requires CAD 150 of cash. After exercise, one hundred twenty-five shares at the theoretical CAD 9.20 are worth CAD 1,150. The increase from the original CAD 1,000 shareholding includes CAD 150 newly paid in.

Calling that CAD 150 increase a profit would count contributed capital as investment performance. The outside-cash account must fall by the same subscription amount. Likewise, comparing CAD 6 only with the old CAD 10 quote ignores that old shares and their entitlement are being separated.

03

Reconcile the repriced old shares with their separate entitlement

At the theoretical ex-rights price, the original one hundred shares are worth CAD 920. Their CAD 80 reduction is paired with an entitlement worth CAD 80 under the same assumptions.

The waterfall starts with the original CAD 1,000 holding, subtracts the CAD 80 repricing and adds the separate theoretical entitlement. Old shares plus their rights remain worth CAD 1,000. The chart creates no cash receipt merely by valuing the right.

The same entitlement value can be checked from the new shares: twenty-five multiplied by the difference between CAD 9.20 and the CAD 6 subscription price equals CAD 80. That value belongs to the existing entitlement; it is not an additional gain created by ignoring the old-share adjustment.

Actual market prices can reflect changes in business prospects, funding needs, issue costs, liquidity and investor demand. They need not equal the theoretical price. This article does not assess the company's capital allocation, expected returns or whether taking up an offer is suitable.

04

Compare complete resources across exercise, sale and lapse

The default holder also has CAD 150 of outside cash. Before detachment, total modeled resources are CAD 1,000 in shares plus CAD 150 cash, or CAD 1,150.

Funded exercise uses that CAD 150 and leaves CAD 1,150 in the enlarged shareholding with no outside cash remaining. The assumed sale alternative retains CAD 920 of old shares and combines the original CAD 150 cash with CAD 80 of rights-sale proceeds, also totaling CAD 1,150.

The lapse scenario provides no compensation. It retains CAD 920 of old shares and the original CAD 150 cash, totaling CAD 1,070. Its CAD 80 difference is the entitlement forfeited within this specifically defined benchmark.

Sale is included only because these hypothetical rights are assumed transferable and sold without costs at their theoretical value. Actual rights may be non-transferable, have a different market value or follow another procedure for unused entitlements. Lapse does not universally imply the exact treatment assumed here.

05

A theoretical value does not fund the subscription

The cash requirement is the number of new shares subscribed multiplied by their subscription price. At the defaults, twenty-five times CAD 6 requires CAD 150. The value of the old shares is not counted as available subscription cash.

If outside cash is reduced to CAD 100, the holder is CAD 50 short of funding the full subscription. The calculator reports that gap and omits the exercised-resource alternative. It does not create an overdraft, sell old shares or assume a deposit will arrive.

The entitlement can still have the same theoretical value when cash is insufficient. Valuation and ability to complete a transaction answer different questions. A sale of rights, if actually permitted and available, is also a separate transaction rather than a deposit already in the account.

This mathematical model permits proportional fractional new-share entitlements without rounding. A real offer's eligibility, whole-share treatment, cash availability, receipt timing and intermediary cut-off need the actual documents. No offer deadline or execution instruction is generated by the tool.

06

Use the discount and ratio matrix as a benchmark, not a price forecast

The matrix changes the subscription discount and the number of old shares required for one new share. It holds the eligible holding and old quote fixed. Every cell reports theoretical total entitlement value, rather than required subscription cash or a promised percentage return.

A zero discount gives zero entitlement value in this unchanged-business, fully subscribed benchmark. A larger discount can increase the value attached to the rights while also creating a larger theoretical adjustment to the old shares. It does not create wealth by itself.

Outside cash does not enter that entitlement-value formula. It determines whether exercise is funded, which is checked separately. The same distinction prevents an attractive-looking right from silently becoming a fully funded household transaction.

For an actual decision, read the offer and verify the eligible holding, ratio, subscription amount, transferability, unused-entitlement treatment and cash deadline. Then evaluate the real business and prices separately. The four charts explain the mechanics and funding condition without turning a capital-raising benchmark into an investment recommendation.
